subject: Bad fit in removal sampling model?

messages.author: d163611c9814a021
messages.subject: Bad fit in removal sampling model?
parts:
Hi All, 

I'm working on models examining avian point-count data using removal sampling in a Bayesian framework. The model is a three-part hierarchical model that estimates single-species detection, abundance, and availability separately. My main question is concerned with understanding covariates on the availability part of the model (things that are changing between visits to a site). 

To examine model fit, I'm calculating a Bayesian p-value for each part of the model separately. I'm running into a lot of trouble getting usable Bayesian p-values for the availability part of my model (almost every time p-value = 0. A good p-value is around 0.5), and I'm wondering if this is because of lack of fit, or if I'm perhaps using the incorrect statistical test in the p-value calculation, or potentially some other reason. Currently, all three Bayesian p-values are calculated using a Freeman-Tukey test statistic. 

Additionally, my mean detection probabilities are almost always quite low in these models (<10%). This is surprising because I have modeled these same data using N-mixture models and get reasonable detection probabilities (>20%). Is the availability structure of the model somehow pulling down my mean detection probability? 

This problem occurs across all species tested (~20). All species are relatively common and abundant at our sites. All analyses use about 5 years of data, with >150 sites surveyed per year. All this is to say, this is not a data sparsity problem. 

I have worked through a simulation of this model, and as far as I can tell, the code is correct. I've included a null version of the model (no covariates on any part of the model) in the attached R file, and have attached data from Green-tailed Towhees in 2018, a very common bird at our sites. 

Running these data through the code in the R file gives these outputs (at 10,000 iterations, 3 chains):
Mean Detection: 0.137 
Mean Availability: 0.81
Mean Abundance: 0.71
P-value Detection: 0.18
P-value Availability: 0
P-value Abundance: 0

Inclusion of covariates and random effects improves the abundance p-value. For example, when I run the full model with both fixed and random effects I get a Bayesian p-value for the abundance part of the model as 0.14. The availability p-value remains at 0. Mean detection decreases to 0.08. 

Any insight on the issues I have highlighted above would be greatly appreciated! 

Thanks for your time,
Martha
